title: Transplant-Sparing Visual Rehabilitation of a Herpetic Corneal Scar Using Refractively Planned Surface Excimer Laser Ablation in a Commercial Pilot: A Case Report
content: Background and Clinical Significance: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis is an important infectious cause of corneal visual impairment. Following resolution of active disease, stromal scarring may produce not only loss of corneal transparency but also irregular astigmatism and optical distortion that persist despite conventional correction. Spectacles, specialty contact lenses, phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK), deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK), and penetrating keratoplasty (PK) represent established rehabilitative options, but each has limitations in selected patients.1–5 This report describes a tissue-preserving, refractively planned surface excimer laser strategy in a patient with a long-standing, visually significant herpetic stromal scar. Case Presentation: A 49-year-old commercial pilot presented with a stable central stromal scar of the left cornea following previous HSV keratitis. His ocular history included corneal debridement nine years earlier and glaucoma drainage-device surgery six years earlier. Uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) was 20/150. Manifest refraction was −1.50 −3.25 × 005, improving corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) to 20/40+. The eye had remained clinically quiescent for several years without evidence of active epithelial or stromal herpetic disease. After evaluation of scar characteristics, corneal architecture, refractive error, visual potential, and occupational requirements, the patient underwent refractively planned surface excimer laser ablation with manual epithelial removal, perioperative systemic antiviral prophylaxis, and intraoperative mitomycin-C. Results: Visual recovery occurred following epithelial healing and continued during postoperative follow-up. At six months, UDVA improved from 20/150 to 20/20. This outcome remained stable through three years of follow-up. No clinical recurrence of HSV keratitis, visually significant postoperative haze, progressive ectasia, or other sight-threatening complication was observed. Corneal topography demonstrated reduced irregular astigmatism and improved optical regularity. The native cornea was preserved, and the patient returned to professional flying without requiring any corneal transplant. Conclusions: In this single carefully selected patient with a long-standing quiescent herpetic stromal scar, refractively planned surface excimer laser ablation was associated with stable 20/20 unaided distance vision through three years while preserving the native cornea. The surgical objective was functional optical rehabilitation rather than complete scar removal or topographic normalization. This case does not establish comparative efficacy or generalizability; prospective studies are required to define appropriate selection criteria, reproducibility, safety, and long-term outcomes.
